# Cetokhila Sutta (MN 16 (PTS MN i 101))

**ID:** MN 16 (PTS MN i 101)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Cetokhila Sutta

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Cetokhila Sutta* (MN 16) is the sixteenth discourse of the *Majjhimanikāya*, delivered by the Buddha to the monks at Jeta's Grove in Anāthapiṇḍika's Park at Sāvatthi [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. The discourse addresses the emotional and psychological impediments that cause a practitioner to become spiritually and emotionally cut off from their community, stunting their growth in the Dhamma and Discipline [Hazra 1994]. Structurally, the text revolves around three main doctrinal sets: the five forms of mental barrenness (*cetokhila*), the five shackles or bondages of the mind (*cetaso vinibandha*), and the four bases of psychic potency (*iddhipāda*) cultivated to overcome them [Gethin 2001; Hazra 1994].

The five *cetokhila* consist of doubt and perplexity regarding the Teacher (the Buddha), the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, and the training (*sikkhā*), as well as anger and discontent directed at one's fellow practitioners (*brahmacārin*) [Khin May Thi 1998; Gethin 2001; Bodhi 2003; Dutt 1924]. According to the commentary (Majjhima-aṭṭhakathā), *cetokhila* signifies a mental stump, rigidity, or rubbish within the heart, comprising four instances of doubt and one of aversion [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. The five *cetaso vinibandha* represent shackles rooted in craving and passion (*rāga*), including attachment to sensual pleasures, to one's physical body, to external forms, indulging in food and sleep, and practicing religious austerity with the wish to be reborn in a celestial realm [Bodhi 2003; Anālayo 2011; Hazra 1994]. Because both sets of obstructions paralyze ardor, exertion, and striving, the sutta presents the four *iddhipāda*s as the transformative remedy [Bodhi 2003; Gethin 2001; Hazra 1994].

 DharmaNexus matches corroborate these close links, registering substantial text reuse between MN 16 and AN 10 (especially §15.1–23.1 with AN 10.14), AN 5, AN 9, DN 33, DN 34, SN 51 (for the *iddhipāda* formula), and Chinese Madhyama Āgama discourse MĀ 206 (ZH_T01_0026_056) [DharmaNexus; Gethin 2001].
